meta: Simone Cantarini's Saint Matthew and the Angel from the mid 1640s, once sold in London as a work by Guercino.
about: An old bearded man in a dark blue cloak reads from a large open book while an angel with braided hair holds an inkwell beside a quill on the table. The angel faces away. Simone Cantarini painted Saint Matthew and the Angel in the mid 1640s. At a Christie's sale in London in 1959 it was catalogued as by Guercino. James O. Belden of Paris and Washington owned it after that, and he gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1972.
credit_line: Gift of James Belden in memory of Evelyn Berry Belden

meta: Isaac Israels's 1882 portrait of a wounded Ghanaian soldier in the Dutch colonial army, who took the name Kees Pop at Elmina.
about: A man in a dark cap with a red headband sits with his right arm in a light cloth sling. A small medal with a blue ribbon is pinned to his jacket, half hidden by the sling. The Rijksmuseum says he was a Ghanaian soldier in the Dutch colonial army in the East Indies. He was given the name Kees Pop when he joined at the former slave fort of Elmina. His African name is unknown. Pop served for twelve years from 1869 and fought in the Aceh War, and the medal is the Aceh medal. Isaac Israels painted him in 1882.

meta: Nicolaes Maes's painting of an old woman dozing over a book, with a bunch of keys on the wall, made around 1655.
about: An old woman in a striped headscarf and dark dress rests her head on one hand, dozing, while an open book lies before her on a red cloth. A bunch of keys hangs from a peg on the wall beside her, and the signature N. MAES sits just above them. The painting was offered at Paris auctions early in the nineteenth century and was bought in, which means it went unsold. It later belonged to Thomas Grove Smith in Worcestershire and then to his son. Agnew's in London bought it in 1919. The Mellon trust purchased it in 1936, and it came to the museum the next year.

meta: Asher B. Durand's 1830 oval portrait of Georgianna Frances Adams, known as Fanny, a granddaughter of John Quincy Adams.
about: Georgianna Frances Adams, called Fanny, was five years old when Asher Durand painted this oval portrait in 1830. She was a granddaughter of John Quincy Adams, the sixth president of the United States. Dark curls tied with blue ribbons frame her face, and she wears a white off-the-shoulder dress with puffed sleeves. Like many children of her time, she died young, only two years later. The Smithsonian American Art Museum says the painting keeps the spirit of a beloved daughter and puts a human face on the Adams family history.

meta: Jacques de Gheyn II's 1603 almost life-size painting of a white Spanish war horse captured at the Battle of Nieuwpoort.
about: Jacques de Gheyn II painted a white Spanish war horse that a groom in a pink tunic and yellow boots leads through a dark interior with two bright windows high on the wall. The horse is shown almost life size. According to the Rijksmuseum, Lodewijk Günther of Nassau captured it from Archduke Albert of Austria at the Battle of Nieuwpoort in 1600 and gave it to Prince Maurits. The picture is dated 1603.

meta: Jean Béraud's view of the rue du Havre in Paris, painted around 1882, with a woman carrying a drum across a wet square.
about: Scaffolding and colorful posters cover a building above a woman in a dark hat and gray skirt who carries a drum across a wet paved square, among men in top hats and other pedestrians. Jean Béraud signed the canvas at lower right and painted this view of the rue du Havre around 1882. It was with Jacques Helft and Company in New York by 1943, when the firm lent it to an exhibition there. Ailsa Mellon Bruce bought it, and her gift brought it to the National Gallery of Art in 1970.

meta: William Merritt Chase's Gathering Autumn Flowers, a seaside meadow scene from the mid 1890s later owned by Paul Mellon.
about: Sunlit grassland stretches toward a band of distant shrubs and blue sea under a cloudy sky. A seated figure in a white dress and bonnet gathers flowers beside a pale green parasol, and two more figures in white stand nearby. William Merritt Chase painted it in the mid 1890s and included it in his own sale at the American Art Galleries in New York in 1896. Louis Ettlinger later owned it. Paul Mellon left it to the National Gallery of Art in 1999, and his wife kept a life interest that was released in 2012.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Johann Ludwig Aberli's 1758 group portrait of five men gathered by a fireplace, now in the Historical Museum of Bern.
about: Five men gather in a wood-paneled room with a gilded mirror, a patterned floor and a red upholstered chair in the foreground. Some sit in conversation while others stand, all dressed in eighteenth-century clothes. The sitters are named as Friedrich Lienhard, Karl Friedrich Bucher, Abraham Wild, Paul Friedrich Otth and Albrecht Herport. Johann Ludwig Aberli painted the group in 1758. It is now in the Historical Museum of Bern.

meta: John Martin's imagined view of a ruined ancient city at twilight, in oil on paper from about 1810 to 1820.
about: Massive Doric-style columns frame the foreground of a broad view over a ruined classical city, with a large amphitheater among tiered buildings below. A hilltop temple and a hazy plain stretch toward the horizon. The Cleveland Museum of Art says the scene is imagined and bathed in the glow of twilight. It reads the detailed, almost archeological interest in Greek or Roman buildings as neoclassical, and the composition that plunges from the foreground into a deep valley as typical of Romantic painting. John Martin made it between about 1810 and 1820.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: Ingres's 1810 portrait of Charles Marcotte d'Argenteuil, painted in Rome for a friend who became one of his key patrons.
about: Charles Marcotte sits with dark hair and a direct gaze, one hand on the arm of a chair draped in red. He was about 36 when Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres painted him in Rome in 1810, and he worked there as inspector general of waters and forests. Marcotte became one of the leading French patrons of the arts and a loyal adviser to Ingres, who later painted portraits of his family, friends and mistress. The portrait was handed down in the Marcotte family before Wildenstein sold it in 1949 to the Kress Foundation, which gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1952.

meta: Thomas Eakins's 1872 painting of the Biglin brothers racing in a scull, later owned by the Whitney Museum of American Art.
about: Two rowers in white sleeveless shirts and blue headscarves pull a red racing scull across calm water, with a paddle wheel steamboat and a crowd on the wooded shore behind them. Thomas Eakins painted it in 1872, and the picture stayed with him. His wife Susan Macdowell Eakins inherited it, and in 1933 she sold it to the Whitney Museum of American Art. Mr. and Mrs. Cornelius Vanderbilt Whitney later bought it from Knoedler, and it came to the National Gallery of Art by bequest in 1953.
credit_line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Cornelius Vanderbilt Whitney

meta: Franz von Lenbach's 1896 portrait of Prince Otto von Bismarck, kept by the painter's widow and given to the Art Institute in 1956.
about: An elderly man in a dark hat, spectacles and a heavy black coat stands in profile with his hands at his sides, painted in loose dark brushwork. Franz von Lenbach made the portrait of Prince Otto von Bismarck in 1896. His second wife Charlotte, known as Lolo, kept it in Munich until at least 1936, according to an inscription on the back. It then passed to Heinrich Karl Knappstein, the German consul general in Chicago, who gave it to Otto K. Eitel. Mr. and Mrs. Eitel gave it to the Art Institute in 1956.
credit_line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Otto K. Eitel

meta: Jacques-Louis David's 1812 full-length portrait of Napoleon in his study at the Tuileries, painted for a Scottish admirer.
about: Napoleon stands full length in a dark blue military coat with gold epaulettes, a red sash and a star-shaped order, one hand resting on a small object. A scroll beside him is marked Code. The scene is his study at the Tuileries, though it is unlikely that he posed. Jacques-Louis David painted it in 1812 as a private commission from the Scottish nobleman Alexander, Marquis of Douglas, later the 10th Duke of Hamilton, who admired Napoleon. It hung at Hamilton Palace until the 1882 sale and was bought for the Kress Foundation in 1954.

meta: Jules Breton's 1860 painting of farm workers harvesting rapeseed, signed at Courrières and later owned by William A. Clark.
about: Farm workers harvest and sort seed in an open field, with a woman in a white blouse and blue apron holding a sieve above a heap of rapeseed. Others bend over the ground or carry sheaves, and a village stands in the distance. Jules Breton signed the canvas at Courrières. Anna Delion of Paris bought it in 1861, and it was sold again the next year under the title La Récolte du colza. William A. Clark of New York bought it later and left it to the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington. The National Gallery of Art acquired it in 2014.

meta: Théo van Rysselberghe's portrait of Denise Maréchal, painted around 1894 as a gift for her grandmother, the artist's mother-in-law.
about: Théo van Rysselberghe painted a young woman in a dark green dress in profile, her long hair built from small touches of color against a background of blue, violet and orange dots. She is Denise Maréchal. The painting was first a gift to her grandmother, who was also the artist's mother-in-law, and a dedication on the back is addressed to that grandmother. Denise later received it herself. After two more gifts it was sold at Sotheby's in London in 2015 and bought by the National Gallery of Art in 2019.

meta: Martin Johnson Heade's 1864 painting of a sailboat on Rio de Janeiro Bay, bought by the National Gallery of Art in 1965.
about: A sailboat crosses a calm bay while surf breaks over rocks in the foreground and a hazy shoreline of hills fades behind. Martin Johnson Heade signed and dated it in 1864. It belonged to John H. Lidgerwood of Morristown, New Jersey, and went to auction with his estate in 1956. The National Gallery of Art bought it from the dealers Victor Spark and Graham Galleries in 1965. Years later the owner of Heade's small Harbor in Brazil said that picture had come from a house called Speedwell in Morristown, in the same collection.

meta: William Glackens's 1906 painting of children and adults in the Luxembourg Gardens, bought by the Corcoran Gallery of Art in 1937.
about: Children play a game with a ball and paddle on a path under green trees while adults in period dress sit on chairs and benches. A building with tall windows rises behind an iron fence. William Glackens painted the Luxembourg Gardens in 1906. By 1937 the picture was with Kraushaar Galleries in New York on consignment from the artist, and the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington bought it there that April. It moved to the National Gallery of Art in 2014.
credit_line: Corcoran Collection (Museum Purchase, William A. Clark Fund, 1937)

meta: Jan Both's Italianate evening landscape with travelers and a donkey, shown in London in 1821 and bought by the National Gallery of Art.
about: Warm evening light falls on a wooded roadside where figures rest and travel along a path with a donkey. Cattle graze near rocky hills. A distant mountain fades into haze. Jan Both painted it in the middle of the seventeenth century. It hung in the Leiden collection of Pieter Cornelis, baron van Leyden, and was sold in Paris in 1804. Alexander Baring had it at Bath House in London by 1821, when it was shown at the British Institution. A later London sale listed it as A Woody Landscape.

meta: Bernardo Bellotto's sunlit view of the Campo di SS. Giovanni e Paolo in Venice, which sold for a very high price in London in 1873.
about: Bernardo Bellotto painted this view of the Campo di SS. Giovanni e Paolo in Venice. A Gothic brick church stands on the right and an ornamented marble facade in the distance, with a bronze equestrian statue near the church and gondolas on the water. At a London sale in 1873 it was sold with a companion view of the Piazza San Marco, which has not been traced. The Earl of Dudley paid 3,360 pounds, a price the historian Gerald Reitlinger called enormous for the time. Peter A. B. Widener had it after the earl's sale in 1892, and the National Gallery of Art received it in 1942.

meta: Johan Laurentz Jensen's flower painting of primulas and beech leaves in a Greek vase, made at the vicarage of Højelse in 1844.
about: Primulas in purple and orange sit in a dark footed vase with handles, mixed with white lily of the valley and fresh beech leaves. A label on the back says Johan Laurentz Jensen painted it in the vicarage at Højelse on 28 May 1844, using flowers and a vase from the vicarage. The label then lists the owners. The vicar H. V. Nyholm had it first, and it went to his son, a pharmacist in Skanderborg, and on through the family. It was offered at auction in Copenhagen in 2005 but did not sell.

meta: Sébastien Bourdon's portrait of Countess Ebba Sparre, probably made for Queen Christina of Sweden and later owned by the dukes of Orléans.
about: Sébastien Bourdon painted a woman in a blue silk gown with full white sleeves, a pearl necklace and a blue ribbon in her hair, holding a small bouquet at the lower edge. The National Gallery of Art says it was probably commissioned by Christina, Queen of Sweden. An inventory of the queen's goods to be sent to Rome includes it. It passed to Cardinal Decio Azzolini, then to his nephew, who sold it in 1696 to Livio Odescalchi. Odescalchi's heir sold it through Pierre Crozat to the Duke of Orléans in 1721.

meta: Henri Martin's Woman in Profile, a seated woman before tall trees painted around 1889 in short strokes of pure color.
about: Slender tree trunks dappled with green stand behind a woman in profile who faces left, her dark hair gathered at the back by a black ribbon and a small blue flower. She wears a loose grey dress. Henri Martin painted her around 1889, just as he was beginning to develop his mature style. The Cleveland Museum of Art points to the short, thick strokes of pure color on figure and background, and to trees built from small hatching strokes into nearly abstract shapes. Martin was celebrated in his lifetime and received commissions for large decorations in Paris, among them the Sorbonne and the Hôtel de Ville.

meta: Thomas Sully's 1810 portrait of Joseph Dugan, owned by the sitter's great-grand-niece before it came to the National Gallery of Art.
about: Joseph Dugan sits with curly white hair, wearing a dark green coat over a cream waistcoat and a white cravat. He holds gold seals in one hand while the other rests on a carved wooden chair arm. Thomas Sully painted the portrait in 1810. The sitter's great-grand-niece, Mrs. Margaret B. Dohan of Philadelphia, owned it, and Herbert Lee Pratt had bought it by 1917. Pratt's collection at Glen Cove, Long Island, was catalogued that year. His gift brought the portrait to the National Gallery of Art in 1945.

meta: Gabriel Huquier's ink and wash rococo design of an enthroned Chinese deity among topiary, made in 1730.
about: An enthroned Chinese figure sits among topiary shown in perspective, while figures on steps to the right and left pay homage. Trees enframe the scene. Above and below, arabesques made of herms and medallions are drawn as if seated, and scrollwork and crossed trophies surround the whole. Gabriel Huquier made the ink and wash design in 1730 in the rococo style. The Cooper Hewitt gives it the title Chinese Deity.

meta: Augustin de Saint-Aubin's 1753 oil sketch of Laban searching for his stolen gods, made for a competition at the Royal Academy in Paris.
about: A bearded figure in a white turban and flowing robes stands in a tent among attendants and seated women, with a kneeling figure in the foreground. Augustin de Saint-Aubin made this oil sketch for a special competition held by the Royal Academy in Paris in 1753. The Cleveland Museum of Art says the sketch was well received and won him first place among three finalists. His final canvas, now in the Louvre, did not win the award. The subject comes from the book of Genesis. After 14 years working for Laban, Jacob fled with his wife Rachel, Laban's daughter, who had stolen her father's idols before they left.
credit_line: Gift of Ruth and Sherman E. Lee in memory of their parents, George B. and Inez W. Ward, and Emery and Adelia Lee

meta: Robert Delaunay's 1914 Political Drama, a circular composition of color rings in oil and collage, once owned by Sonia Delaunay.
about: Concentric rings and rainbow-like arcs of saturated color radiate from a central target, with two stylized human figures standing nearby. Robert Delaunay made the work in 1914 in oil and collage on cardboard. His wife Sonia Delaunay owned it and lent it to an exhibition in Leverkusen. The Galerie Fricker in Paris sold it in 1957 to Mr. and Mrs. Joseph H. Hazen of New York. Their foundation gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1971.
credit_line: Gift of the Joseph H. Hazen Foundation, Inc.

meta: A small round view of the facade of St. Peter's in Rome, attributed to Johann Wilhelm Baur, who lived in the city from 1630 to 1637.
about: A circular painting shows the facade and dome of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. An obelisk stands in the foreground of a busy piazza where carriages, horses and pedestrians move. The Karlsruhe museum describes it as a small architectural view of one of the seven pilgrimage churches of Rome. Johann Wilhelm Baur painted such views while he lived in the city between 1630 and 1637. It is in gouache and chalk on parchment mounted on wood.

meta: The Master of the Die's engraving Venus Complains to Jupiter, dated 1520, with Jupiter enthroned among clouds.
about: Jupiter sits among clouds at the centre with an eagle before him, and Hermes stands at the left in a winged helmet with a staff. Venus arrives from the right on a chariot led by doves. Behind them Venus talks with Hermes, and below Hermes is shown again in a hilly landscape. A narrative inscription runs along the bottom. The print is attributed to the Master of the Die and dated 1520.

meta: Gustave Moreau's The Mystic Flower, painted around 1890 as the closing work of his Cycle of Man.
about: A crowned, haloed woman in a red and gold robe sits on a large pale flower, holding a tall cross while a dove hovers above her. Below, haloed figures kneel among rocks. Gustave Moreau painted The Mystic Flower in oil around 1890. It was inspired by Carpaccio's Apotheosis of Saint Ursula, which Moreau copied during his stay in Venice. At 2.53 metres tall, it closed his Cycle of Man, which shows the importance of sacrifice by heroic figures.

meta: Antoon Derkinderen's 1901 painting of the Argonauts building their ship Argo on a beach, bequeathed to the Rijksmuseum in 1944.
about: Argonauts on the quay point out to sea while a golden ship with a carved serpent-headed prow is built on the beach at left. A bearded man sleeps in the foreground. A few bathers swim in the water, two columns mark the entrance to the bay in the distance, and in the clouds Apollo drives his sun chariot. Antoon Derkinderen painted The Building of the Argo in 1901. His widow, Johanna Henriëtte Derkinderen-Besier, left it to the Rijksmuseum in 1944 with 177 other objects.

meta: Gustave Caillebotte's Skiffs, a sunlit river scene from 1877 with a second signature that was probably not the artist's.
about: Two men in white shirts and straw hats row light wooden skiffs across a sunlit green river, with dappled reflections on the water and leafy trees along the banks. Gustave Caillebotte painted Skiffs in 1877, and the date is written at upper right. A second signature at lower left was probably added by someone other than the artist in imitation of his studio stamp. Caillebotte died without children, and the painting stayed with his family until 1966. Wildenstein sold it that year to Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon, who gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1985.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Edward John Poynter's The Golden Age from 1875, bequeathed to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2002 by Suzette Morton Davidson.
about: A nude youth climbs a wooden ladder to pick golden fruit from a tree, while below him a second figure in a dark cap and white wrap holds up a fruit beside a woven basket. Edward John Poynter kept the painting and lent it to a London exhibition in 1875, together with The Festival. The two works reappeared at Colnaghi in London. Suzette Morton Davidson bought them in 1973, and she bequeathed The Golden Age to the Art Institute in 2002, with her husband Eugene keeping a life interest.

meta: Jacques-Emile Blanche's The Traveler, a theatrical portrait of his favorite model Désirée Manfred, painted around 1890.
about: A letter lies at the sitter's feet beside the glove she would have removed to open it. Her stoic expression suggests that the contents were grave, even ominous. Jacques-Emile Blanche painted his favorite model, Désirée Manfred, as an elegant and mysterious traveler around 1890. The Art Institute of Chicago says this is no real moment, since the costume and scenery turn her into a character. Behind her a rider in a red coat sits on a grey horse. Blanche painted Manfred in various guises, female and male, following genre portraits made popular by Manet.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection
